title: proposal-evaluation
description: What /actian-ux-proposal --evaluate writes: the framing, the product read, the scope, and the decisions the ticket forces, with no options, no comparison and no picks. Completed into a proposal-data.json by adding keys, never by renaming one.

meta.description: Document-level context printed in the title strip and the provenance comment

title.description: What was asked, in the requester's terms and ten words at most: the page H1 and the document title. It names the ask, never the answer or the constraints on it
examples: DIP-I-496: show role and permission for a logged-in user

ticket.description: Ticket or story id the proposal answers

date.description: Authoring date, YYYY-MM-DD, printed in the title strip. Never a render-time clock, so a re-render is byte-identical

apps.description: App slugs the ticket lives in, printed in the title strip

items.description: An app slug the vendored app-context knows

prompt.description: The request the document answers, kept in the provenance comment only
examples: Propose a design for this ticket: DIP-I-496

model.description: Model that authored the document, provenance comment only

skill.description: Always actian-ux-proposal (design-proposal before 2026.9.59, still accepted); lets a reader tell this file from a flow-data.json

stage.description: Which stage of the pipeline this file is at. Absent means proposal, which is what every file authored before the evaluation stage existed is, so nothing needs touching. Only --evaluate writes "evaluation".

source.description: The ticket this proposal answers, as it arrived. Filled from pasted text today and by a fetcher later; nothing downstream cares which

id.description: The ticket id in that system

url.description: A link a reader can follow; omitted for a pasted ticket. Never rendered as a link, the document is offline

title.description: The ticket's own title, in its words
examples: Show role and permission for a logged-in user

body.description: The ticket text the proposal was written from, kept so a reader can check the proposal against it
examples: As a user I want to see which permission group I belong to.

context.description: Where the ticket lives and the question it asks, from the app-context and whatever the request attached

question.description: The design question in one sentence, as said in Step 1
examples: How does a logged-in user see their assigned role and permission group?

ask.description: What was asked, in one or two plain sentences from the ticket: who needs what, and why, plus any direction the request added. It opens the document under The ask, above the answer. Optional so older files still render; the validator asks for it
examples: A logged-in user cannot see which permission group they belong to, so they cannot find the guidelines that go with it.

product.description: Facts about how the product handles this today, one line each: the anchor surface, the data model behind it, what an admin and a user see. Three to six is the useful range and six is the ceiling; fewer than three usually means the product read stopped early. Facts, not a paragraph

examples: A permission group is a Group record in Administration.
A user can belong to more than one group.

sources.description: Where the product read came from: app-context facts and attachments, one line each

items.description: One source, prefixed app-context: or attachment:

gap.description: One sentence naming what the substrate has no capture of, when the anchor surface is uncaptured; absent otherwise
examples: The account dropdown has no capture in app-context.

scope.description: What the proposal is for and what it deliberately leaves out. Non-goals are what stops a reviewer scoping the work sideways; they are as load-bearing as the goals.

goals.description: One to four things the change must achieve, each in one line, drawn from the ticket rather than invented

examples: A user can read their permission group without leaving the dropdown.

nonGoals.description: One to four things this change deliberately does not do, each in one line; the reviewer reads these to know what not to ask for

examples: Editing a permission group from the dropdown; assignment stays in Administration.

research.description: What the research found, in four lanes (competitors, designSystems, ours, yours), bounded to four findings a lane with a source each; always present, and honest when it did not run

lanes.description: The lanes that were asked for at the Step 3 gate. Absent on a file written before the lanes existed, which is read as one competitor sweep

items.description: One lane: competitors (the product space), designSystems (the public canon), ours (the Actian substrate), yours (references the reader supplied at the gate)

refs.description: The references the reader pasted at the gate, one line each: a URL, a product and screen, or a file they attached. Required when the yours lane ran, and every yours finding must cite one

items.description: One reference, as the reader gave it
examples: the Okta admin console, groups page

ran.description: true when the web research ran; false when it was turned off or unavailable

findings.description: At most four findings a lane (validator-enforced); empty when ran is false

items.description: One finding, with the lane it came from and its source

lane.description: Which lane found it. Absent on a file written before the lanes existed, which is read as competitors

claim.description: One sentence in the reader's words
examples: Role sits under the name as a secondary identity signal, never above it.

source.description: The product, article, substrate file or reference the claim comes from, as text (the document loads nothing). A finding in the ours lane must prefix it with a substrate kind (app-context: guideline: pattern: accessibility: foundations: content: tokens:); a finding in the yours lane must repeat one of research.refs exactly
examples: SaaS Permissions and Roles UX Patterns, SaaSUI Design
the Okta admin console, groups page

skippedBecause.description: Required when ran is false (validator-enforced): why the research did not run
examples: no web search in this session

openQuestions.description: At most four things the proposal does not settle and that do NOT change any pick: a rabbit hole is a detail of a chosen option worth flagging so nobody falls in, an open question is something a reader has to decide later. Anything that would change a pick is that decision's blocker instead. Omit the field when there are none; never invent one.

items.description: One rabbit hole or one open question

kind.description: Which of the two this is

text.description: One or two sentences, in the reader's words
examples: Truncating a long group list needs a hover affordance the dropdown does not have today.

decisions.description: One entry per question the ticket forces that a reader could answer differently. At most four, and one is the common case.

examples.question: Where does an admin see a share's real reach?

items.description: A decision this ticket forces, named but not yet answered.

examples.question: Where does an admin see a share's real reach?

id.description: Slug unique in the file; the anchor a reader and the flow bridge address the decision by

part.description: What this decision builds, in two to four of the product's words, as Step 4 named it. Optional here; the finished document asks for it

question.description: The decision as a question in one sentence
examples: How does a user see which group they belong to?
